newsitem.title: UK: Access to grain supply seen as future trade issue.
newsitem.headline: Access to grain supply seen as future trade issue.

text.p: Future trade negotiations may focus on giving consumers access to scarce grain supplies in the same way that previous ones sought to give producers access to importing markets, said Lester Brown, president of the Washington-based Worldwatch Institute.

The politics of scarcity and increasing demand for grain would cause a shift in the terms of trade in favour of encouraging output in rural producing areas, Brown told a conference on the changing world of agriculture organised by Oppenheimer International.

Grain output is now hitting its three natural constraints - water, the ability of plants to absorb fertiliser and changes in climate, he stated, noting that despite studies "there is no idea of the effect of global warming".
Brown said Saudi Arabia illustrated the growing importance of water as a natural resource and how grain is used as a currency to balance a country's water needs.
Saudi Arabia had to cut high wheat support prices which caused surplus output and placed a strain on water reserves.

Brown reiterated earlier warnings on the growth in food consumption in China. China does not have sufficient land to sustain its recent economic growth rate and has a water shortage with over 300 cities declaring water a scarce commodity.

The combination of China's land and water shortage means it will find it difficult to increase grain production, said Brown. Even reduced single digit economic growth would generate enormous demand for grains.
"I don't believe anybody can supply China's needs," said Brown, who believes real grain prices need to rise.

Brown repeated forecasts that China's grain imports will rise sharply, especially if its 1.2 billion population continues to eat more meat at the expense of grain, because of high cattle grain consumption.
